scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Monitoring ticket #9163: the NOC got a transient alert and now believes a core
backbone router (R6, possibly R7) "crashed and is down," and that traffic which
transits the core toward the far end of the network is being black-holed. They
want the crashed backbone router confirmed and recovered. Please confirm the fault.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. R6 and R7 are up: their ospfd processes are
  running, the R6<->R7 OSPF adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
  67.x, 70.x) are present in the backbone. PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
  (120.1.1.10) end to end with 0% loss, so the core is forwarding. The correct
  answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a backbone
  router crash that is not occurring (cf. kath5-r6-ospfd-down / kath5-r7-ospfd-down,
  where a core daemon IS down).

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- a crashed backbone router
(R6/R7) black-holing core traffic -- is NOT reproducible: R6 and R7 are up, their
ospfd is running, the R6<->R7 adjacency is Full, and the R7-region prefixes (17.x,
67.x, 70.x) remain in the backbone. End to end, PC0 (20.1.1.10) reaches PC12
(120.1.1.10) with 0% loss, which requires the core to be forwarding -- inconsistent
with a crashed transit router on the path.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the backbone routers are up and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent checks R6/R7 liveness (ospfd
running, adjacency Full, prefixes present) and exercises the PC0<->PC12 path -- all
healthy -- and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a crashed router -- declaring
R6 or R7 down or restarting its frr to satisfy the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
No core router crash is present. Both backbone nodes R6 and R7 are up, forwarding, and fully participating in OSPF. Evidence: systemd shows FRRouting active on R6 and R7. OSPF adjacencies are Full on R6 to R4 (46.1.1.1 via eth0), R5 (56.1.1.1 via eth1), and R7 (67.1.1.2 via eth2); R7 is Full to R6 (67.1.1.1 via eth0). Routing tables on both routers contain expected OSPF-learned routes, including R6’s route to 70.0.0.0/8 via R7. Data-plane checks confirm transit: pings to R7’s 70.1.1.1 from R6, R4, and R5 succeed end-to-end, demonstrating core forwarding across R6. End-user reachability pc0↔pc12 shows 0% loss with normal RTTs.

Mechanism of the alert: OSPF neighbor up-times are ~1 minute across multiple neighbors, indicating a recent control-plane restart or adjacency reset that would have triggered a transient monitoring alarm. However, the network has since reconverged; there is no ongoing black-holing.

Localization: Core OSPF on R6 (eth0/eth1/eth2) and R7 (eth0) are healthy; the R6–R7 link Y is operating normally.

Root cause: A short-lived OSPF flap or FRR reload occurred recently, but it self-recovered.

Corrective fix: No remediation required now. Close the outage ticket as cleared. Optionally, review FRR logs for the timeframe of the alert to pinpoint the trigger and consider adding debounce/hysteresis on OSPF-down alerts to avoid false positives from brief control-plane resets.
